records.question: What are NVIDIA's main revenue streams and business segments?
records.answer:
NVIDIA's main revenue streams and business segments are categorized into two primary segments: **Compute & Networking** and **Graphics**.

1. **Compute & Networking Segment**: This segment includes NVIDIA's Data Center accelerated computing and networking platforms, AI solutions, and software, as well as automotive platforms and solutions for autonomous and electric vehicles. The Data Center platform focuses on accelerating compute-intensive workloads, such as AI and data processing, and is deployed in various environments including cloud and on-premises data centers. This segment has seen significant revenue growth driven by demand for accelerated computing and AI solutions, particularly from the Blackwell architecture (Chunk 1, Chunk 3).

2. **Graphics Segment**: This segment encompasses GeForce GPUs for gaming and PCs, as well as Quadro/NVIDIA RTX GPUs for enterprise workstation graphics. The Graphics segment serves a variety of markets, including gaming and professional visualization, and is supported by NVIDIA's partnerships with independent software vendors to optimize applications for their GPUs (Chunk 1, Chunk 2).

Overall, NVIDIA's revenue is significantly driven by the demand for its Data Center computing platforms and its Graphics products, with a notable focus on AI and accelerated computing technologies (Chunk 3).

In addition to serving the growing number of gamers, the market for PC GPUs is expanding because of the growing population of live streamers, broadcasters, artists, and creators. With the advent of generative and agentic AI, we expect a broader set of PC users to choose NVIDIA GPUs for running these applications locally on their PC, which is critical for privacy, latency, and cost-sensitive AI applications.
Professional artists, architects and designers use NVIDIA partner products accelerated with our GPUs and software platform for a range of creative, engineering, and design use cases, such as creating visual effects in movies or designing buildings and products. In addition, generative and agentic AI is expanding the market for our workstation-class GPUs, as more enterprise customers develop and deploy AI applications with their data on-premises.
Headquartered in Santa Clara, California, NVIDIA was incorporated in California in April 1993 and reincorporated in Delaware in April 1998.
Our Businesses
We report our business results in two segments.
The Compute & Networking segment includes our Data Center accelerated computing and networking platforms and AI solutions and software, and Automotive platforms and autonomous and electric vehicle solutions including software.
The Graphics segment includes GeForce GPUs for gaming and PCs, and Quadro/NVIDIA RTX GPUs for enterprise workstation graphics.
Our Markets
We specialize in markets where our computing and AI infrastructure platforms can provide tremendous acceleration for applications. These platforms incorporate processors, interconnects, software, algorithms, systems, and services to deliver unique value. Our platforms address four large markets where our expertise is critical: Data Center, Gaming, Professional Visualization, and Automotive.
Data Center
The NVIDIA Data Center platform is focused on accelerating compute-intensive workloads, such as AI, data processing, graphics, robotics, and scientific computing, delivering superior total cost of ownership relative to conventional CPU-only approaches. It is deployed in cloud, hyperscale, on-premises and edge data centers. The platform consists of data center compute and networking infrastructure offerings typically delivered to customers as rack-scale systems, subsystems, or modules, along with software and services.
Our Data Center infrastructure systems include supercomputing platforms and servers, bringing together our higher performance, energy efficient GPUs, CPUs, interconnects, and fully optimized AI and HPC software stacks. In addition, they include a growing body of acceleration libraries, AI models and training data sets, APIs, SDKs, and domain-specific application frameworks.
Our networking offerings include NVLink interconnects and switches, end

, image quality, and interactivity, as well as the next generation of our DLSS technology powered by a new transformer model architecture. In fiscal year 2026, we launched and scaled Blackwell architecture for gaming and GeForce NOW.
Professional Visualization
We serve the Professional Visualization market by working closely with independent software vendors, or ISVs, to optimize their offerings for NVIDIA GPUs. Our GPU computing platform enhances productivity and introduces new capabilities for critical workflows in many fields, such as design, engineering, and digital content creation across a wide range of industry verticals. Additionally, the increasing number of generative and agentic AI applications is giving rise to the need for the enhanced AI and data processing capabilities of our RTX PRO GPUs.
Many leading 3D design and content creation applications developed by our ecosystem partners support RTX, allowing professionals to accelerate and transform their workflows with NVIDIA RTX PRO GPUs and software. As these applications increasingly integrate AI, these GPUs are used and leverage the same Tensor Core technology found in our Data Center solutions.
Automotive
Automotive is comprised of platform solutions for automated driving from the cloud to the car. Leveraging our technology leadership in AI and building on long-standing relationships across several hundred automotive ecosystem partners, we are delivering a full stack end-to-end solution for the AV market under the DRIVE Hyperion platform. This platform consists of development infrastructure, high-performance, energy efficient DRIVE AGX computing hardware

Advancing the NVIDIA accelerated computing platform.
Our accelerated computing platform can solve complex problems in significantly less time and with lower power consumption than alternative computational approaches. Our Company and Our Businesses
NVIDIA pioneered accelerated computing to help solve the most challenging computational problems. Since our original focus on PC graphics, we have expanded to several other large and important computationally intensive fields. Fueled by the sustained demand for exceptional 3D graphics and the scale of the gaming market, NVIDIA has leveraged its GPU architecture to create platforms for scientific computing, AI, data science, autonomous vehicles, robotics, and digital twin applications. NVIDIA is now a data center scale AI infrastructure company reshaping all industries.

Contracts with Multiple Performance Obligations
Our contracts may contain more than one performance obligation. Judgment is required in determining whether each performance obligation within a customer contract is distinct. Except for License and Development Arrangements, NVIDIA products and services function on a standalone basis and do not require a significant amount of integration or interdependency. Therefore, multiple performance obligations contained within a customer contract are considered distinct and are not combined for revenue recognition purposes.
We allocate the total transaction price to each distinct performance obligation in an arrangement with multiple performance obligations on a relative standalone selling price basis. In most cases, we can establish standalone selling price based on directly observable prices of products or services sold separately in comparable circumstances to similar customers. If standalone selling price is not directly observable, such as when we do not sell a product or service separately, we determine standalone selling price based on market data and other observable inputs.

records.question: What AI-related risks does NVIDIA identify in its 10-K?
records.answer:
NVIDIA identifies several AI-related risks in its 10-K filing:

1. **Regulatory Scrutiny**: The company notes that its position in AI markets has led to increased interest from regulators worldwide, which could result in compliance costs and restrictions. For instance, the EU AI Act, effective August 1, 2024, may impact NVIDIA's ability to train, deploy, or release AI models in the EU (Chunk 2).

2. **Compliance Costs**: Changes to laws and regulations, particularly concerning AI technologies, could lead to materially greater compliance costs and further restrictions on NVIDIA's ability to operate its business (Chunk 2).

3. **Infrastructure Limitations**: The availability of data centers, energy, and capital to support the buildout of NVIDIA's AI infrastructure by customers and partners is crucial. Any shortages in these resources could negatively impact future revenue and financial performance (Chunk 3).

4. **Competition and Market Dynamics**: The competitive landscape for AI technologies is intense, and competitors may offer cheaper or more functional products, which could result in lower demand for NVIDIA's offerings (Chunk 4).

These excerpts collectively highlight the regulatory, operational, and competitive risks associated with NVIDIA's AI-related business activities.

Examples include generative AI, which can create new content such as text, code, images, audio, video, molecule structures, and recommendation systems; and agentic AI where systems of AI models work in concert to automatically complete a task.

records.question: What is NVIDIA's data center segment revenue and growth?
records.answer:
NVIDIA's data center segment revenue for fiscal year 2026 experienced significant growth. Specifically, revenue from Data Center computing grew by 59%, driven by demand for the Blackwell computing platform. Additionally, revenue from Data Center networking grew by 142%, attributed to the introduction and continued ramp of NVLink compute fabric for GB200 and GB300 systems, as well as the growth of Ethernet and InfiniBand platforms. records.question: What supply chain and manufacturing risks does NVIDIA face?
records.answer:
NVIDIA faces several supply chain and manufacturing risks, as highlighted in the provided context:

1. **Availability of Resources**: The availability of data centers, energy, and capital is crucial for building NVIDIA's AI infrastructure. Any shortage of these resources could negatively impact future revenue and financial performance (Chunk 1, Chunk 3).

2. **Complexity of Expanding Energy Capacity**: Expanding energy capacity to meet demand is described as a complex, multi-year process that involves significant regulatory, technical, and construction challenges (Chunk 1, Chunk 3).

3. **Access to Capital**: Less-capitalized companies may struggle to secure financing for large-scale infrastructure projects, which could delay deployments or reduce the scale of AI adoption (Chunk 1, Chunk 3).

4. **Supply Constraints**: NVIDIA anticipates supply constraints to be a headwind for its Gaming segment in the first quarter of fiscal year 2027 and beyond. This includes challenges in managing multiple suppliers and variations in production planning, execution, and logistics (Chunk 1).

5. **Inventory Management**: The integration of new suppliers and increased purchase volumes may lead to higher inventory levels. NVIDIA may incur inventory provisions or impairments if supply commitments exceed demand (Chunk 1).

6. **Manufacturing Delays**: The company is increasing U.S.-based manufacturing but may experience delays or difficulties in scaling production as planned. The ability to ramp production supply to required volumes is dependent on the domestic manufacturing ecosystem (Chunk 1).

7. **Product Transitions**: The complexity of product transitions can lead to challenges as NVIDIA ships both new and prior architecture products simultaneously, which complicates inventory and demand management (Chunk 1).

8. **Long Manufacturing Lead Times**: Long lead times and uncertain supply and capacity availability can adversely affect NVIDIA's ability to meet demand (Chunk 4).

These factors collectively pose significant risks to NVIDIA's supply chain and manufacturing operations, potentially impacting its financial results and market position.

records.question: What export control and regulatory restrictions affect NVIDIA?
records.answer:
NVIDIA faces several export control and regulatory restrictions that could materially impact its business, operating results, and financial condition. The key points include:

1. **Export Controls on GPUs**: The U.S. Government (USG) has imposed export controls restricting certain gaming GPUs, and there is a risk that these controls could expand to additional gaming products. This could disrupt a significant portion of NVIDIA's supply and distribution chain and negatively impact sales to markets outside China, including the U.S. and Europe (Chunk 1).

2. **Impact on Data Center Products**: Export controls restricting the sale of data center GPUs may negatively affect demand for NVIDIA's networking products used in servers containing these GPUs. There is also a possibility that the USG may impose further export controls on networking products, which could limit the ability of downstream parties to create large clusters for frontier model training (Chunk 1).

3. **Disruption of Supply Chain**: Export controls could disrupt NVIDIA's supply chain and distribution channels, negatively impacting its ability to serve demand in various markets, including those outside China (Chunk 2).

4. **Compliance Burdens**: Repeated changes in export control rules are likely to impose compliance burdens on NVIDIA and its customers, which could materially impact the business. These changes may also lead to excess inventory or related supply charges (Chunk 2).

5. **Regulatory Scrutiny**: NVIDIA is under increased scrutiny from regulators worldwide, including inquiries regarding its sales and compliance with export controls, particularly in relation to its acquisition of Mellanox. Non-compliance could result in financial penalties or restrictions on business operations (Chunk 2).

6. **Potential Licensing Requirements**: The USG may impose licensing requirements that could benefit competitors and make NVIDIA's technical support efforts more cumbersome. Such requirements could also discourage customers in certain regions from purchasing NVIDIA products (Chunk 4).

7. **Geopolitical Tensions**: The increasing strategic importance of AI and rising geopolitical tensions may lead to further changes in export control rules, potentially subjecting a wider range of NVIDIA's products to restrictions (Chunk 4).

Overall, these export controls and regulatory restrictions pose significant risks to NVIDIA's ability to operate effectively in global markets and could adversely affect its financial performance.

records.question: What are NVIDIA's cybersecurity risk management policies?
records.answer:
NVIDIA has implemented several cybersecurity risk management policies and practices designed to proactively prevent, reduce the impact of, and reactively address cybersecurity incidents. These include:

1. **Infrastructure and Systems**: They have established infrastructure, systems, policies, and procedures aimed at managing material risks from cybersecurity threats. This is supported by processes for assessing and identifying risks (Chunk 1).

2. **Information Security Management Programs**: Their programs follow frameworks such as the ISO 27001 international standard for information security management, and they regularly evaluate and evolve their security measures (Chunk 1).

3. **Vendor Risk Assessment**: NVIDIA has a vendor risk assessment process that involves distributing and reviewing supplier questionnaires to evaluate cybersecurity risks associated with third parties that have access to sensitive company information. They also assess high-risk suppliers for conformance to industry standards (Chunk 1).

4. **Training and Policies**: The company has implemented cybersecurity and data privacy training and policies to respond to new global privacy and cybersecurity laws and to mitigate significant cybersecurity threats (Chunk 1).

5. **Governance Oversight**: The Board of Directors oversees information security matters, with the Audit Committee reviewing the adequacy and effectiveness of the company's information security policies and practices (Chunk 1).

These policies are part of a comprehensive approach to integrate cybersecurity risk management into their overall risk management systems and processes.

Risk management and strategy
We have in place certain infrastructure, systems, policies, and procedures that are designed to proactively prevent or reduce the impact of, and reactively address circumstances that arise when, events such as a cybersecurity incident occur. These include processes for assessing, identifying, and managing material risks from cybersecurity threats. Our information security management programs generally follow certain processes outlined in frameworks such as the ISO 27001 international standard for information security management and we evaluate and evolve our security measures as appropriate.
We consult with external parties, such as cybersecurity firms and risk management and governance experts, on risk management and strategy.
Identifying, assessing, and managing cybersecurity risk is integrated into our overall risk management systems and processes, and we have in place cybersecurity and data privacy training and policies designed to (a) respond to new requirements in global privacy and cybersecurity laws and (b) prevent, detect, respond to, mitigate and recover from identified and significant cybersecurity threats.
We also have a vendor risk assessment process consisting of, depending on the nature and sensitivity of the supplier and data they process on our behalf, the distribution and review of supplier questionnaires designed to help us evaluate cybersecurity risks that we may encounter when working with third parties that have access to confidential and other sensitive company information. We take steps to review that such vendors have implemented data privacy and security controls that help mitigate the cybersecurity risks associated with these vendors, depending on the nature and sensitivity of the supplier and data they process on our behalf. We routinely assess our high-risk suppliers’ conformance to industry standards (e.g., ISO 27001, ISO 28001, and C-TPAT), and we evaluate them for additional information, product, and physical security requirements.

records.answer:
NVIDIA protects its intellectual property (IP) primarily through a combination of patents, trademarks, trade secrets, employee and third-party nondisclosure agreements, and licensing arrangements. According to the context provided, "We rely primarily on a combination of patents, trademarks, trade secrets, employee and third-party nondisclosure agreements, and licensing arrangements to protect our IP in the United States and internationally" (Chunk 2).

The GPU was initially used to simulate human imagination, enabling the virtual worlds of video games and films. This form of AI, in which software writes itself by learning from large amounts of data, can serve as the brain of computers, robots, and self-driving cars that can perceive, understand and reason about the world. Our contracts may contain more than one performance obligation. Judgment is required in determining whether each performance obligation within a customer contract is distinct. We allocate the total transaction price to each distinct performance obligation in an arrangement with multiple performance obligations on a relative standalone selling price basis. In most cases, we can establish standalone selling price based on directly observable prices of products or services sold separately in comparable circumstances to similar customers. If standalone selling price is not directly observable, such as when we do not sell a product or service separately, we determine standalone selling price based on market data and other observable inputs.

records.question: What are NVIDIA's main product lines including H100 and Blackwell?
records.answer:
NVIDIA's main product lines include:

1. **Blackwell Architecture**: Launched in fiscal year 2025, it is a full set of data center scale infrastructure that includes GPUs, CPUs, DPUs, interconnects, switch chips, systems, and networking adapters. Blackwell excels at processing generative AI and accelerated computing workloads with market-leading performance and efficiency. In fiscal year 2026, NVIDIA introduced the Blackwell Ultra platform, optimized for agentic, reasoning, and physical AI (Chunk 1).

2. **H100 Tensor Core GPU**: Although the provided context does not explicitly mention the H100, it is typically associated with NVIDIA's data center offerings and AI capabilities, which align with the advancements made in the Blackwell architecture and the overall focus on AI and accelerated computing.

3. **GeForce RTX GPUs**: These are designed for gaming desktop and laptop PCs and include features like ray tracing technology and deep learning super sampling (DLSS) to enhance gaming experiences. The Blackwell architecture also introduced the GeForce RTX 50 Series family of GPUs (Chunk 1).

4. **NVIDIA AI Enterprise Software**: This is a comprehensive suite of enterprise-grade AI software that supports various applications across industries (Chunk 4).

5. **NVIDIA DRIVE Platform**: This includes solutions for automated driving, leveraging AI technology for full self-driving capabilities (Chunk 5).

These product lines reflect NVIDIA's strategy to serve diverse markets, including data centers, gaming, professional visualization, and automotive.

Revenue growth in fiscal year 2026 was driven by data center compute and networking platforms for accelerated computing and AI solutions. Our Blackwell architectures represented the majority of our Data Center revenue.

records.question: What are NVIDIA's customer concentration risks?
records.answer:
NVIDIA's customer concentration risks are highlighted in the following excerpts:

1. **Direct Customer Concentration**: For fiscal year 2026, sales to one direct customer represented 22% of total revenue and sales to another direct customer represented 14% of total revenue, all primarily attributable to the Compute & Networking segment. This indicates a significant reliance on a limited number of direct customers for revenue (Chunk 2).

2. **Indirect Customer Concentration**: NVIDIA generates a significant amount of its revenue from a limited number of indirect customers, some of whom individually represent 10% or more of total revenue. This trend of concentration may continue, posing a risk if any of these key customers reduce their purchases (Chunk 2).

3. **Overall Revenue Concentration**: The company acknowledges that its revenue is concentrated among a limited number of direct and indirect customers, which could lead to vulnerabilities if any major customer were to experience financial difficulties or change their purchasing behavior (Chunk 2).

These points illustrate that NVIDIA's reliance on a small number of customers for a substantial portion of its revenue creates concentration risks that could impact its financial performance.

records.question: What is NVIDIA's NVLink and networking strategy?
records.answer:
NVIDIA's NVLink and networking strategy focuses on creating high-performance networking solutions that enable data center-scale computing platforms. This includes the development of NVLink interconnects and switches, as well as end-to-end platforms for InfiniBand and Ethernet, which consist of network adapters, cables, DPUs, switch chips, and systems, along with software. This architecture allows for the interconnection of hundreds of thousands of compute nodes, which is essential for handling the increasing demands of AI and HPC workloads.

The strategy is highlighted in the following excerpts:

1. "Our networking offerings include NVLink interconnects and switches, end-to-end platforms for InfiniBand and Ethernet, consisting of network adapters, cables, DPUs, switch chips and systems, as well as software." (Chunk 1)
2. "This has enabled us to architect data center-scale computing platforms that can interconnect up to hundreds of thousands of compute nodes with high-performance networking." (Chunk 1)
3. "Fueled by an expansion in AI and HPC workloads, the data center has become the new unit of computing, with networking as an integral part." (Chunk 1)

Overall, NVIDIA's strategy is to integrate powerful networking capabilities into their data center solutions to enhance performance and scalability for their customers.

records.question: What geographic risks does NVIDIA face related to China and Taiwan?
records.answer:
NVIDIA faces several geographic risks related to China, primarily stemming from export controls and regulatory scrutiny. 

1. **Export Controls**: The U.S. government has imposed export controls that restrict certain gaming GPUs and may expand these controls to additional gaming products. This could disrupt NVIDIA's supply and distribution chain, negatively impacting sales to markets outside China, including the U.S. and Europe. The context states, "Export controls have already and may in the future negatively impact demand for our products and services not only in China, but also in other markets, such as Europe, Latin America, and Southeast Asia" (Chunk 1).

2. **Regulatory Scrutiny**: NVIDIA is under increased interest from regulators worldwide, including in China. The company has received requests for information from various competition regulators regarding its sales and market strategies. This scrutiny could lead to compliance costs and operational restrictions. For instance, "Governments and regulators are also considering, and in certain cases, have imposed restrictions on the hardware, software, and systems used to develop frontier foundation models and generative AI" (Chunk 3).

3. **Impact on Business Operations**: The potential for additional export controls could lead to excess inventory and financial penalties if NVIDIA is found to have violated any applicable laws in China. The context mentions, "Additional export restrictions may not only impact our ability to serve overseas markets, but also provoke responses from foreign governments, including China, that negatively impact our supply chain or our ability to provide our products and services to customers in all markets worldwide" (Chunk 5).

In summary, NVIDIA's geographic risks related to China include the potential for disruptive export controls, increased regulatory scrutiny, and the possibility of retaliatory actions from the Chinese government that could affect its operations and market access.

records.question: What are NVIDIA's main revenue streams and business segments?
records.answer:
NVIDIA's main revenue streams and business segments are categorized into two primary segments: Compute & Networking and Graphics. 

1. **Compute & Networking Segment**: This segment includes Data Center accelerated computing and networking platforms, AI solutions and software, and Automotive platforms for autonomous and electric vehicles. The Data Center platform focuses on accelerating compute-intensive workloads such as AI, data processing, and scientific computing. Revenue growth in this segment has been driven by demand for accelerated computing and AI solutions, particularly from the Blackwell architecture (Chunk 3).

2. **Graphics Segment**: This segment encompasses GeForce GPUs for gaming and PCs, as well as Quadro/NVIDIA RTX GPUs for enterprise workstation graphics. The Graphics segment serves markets such as gaming and professional visualization, where NVIDIA's GPUs enhance productivity and capabilities in design, engineering, and digital content creation (Chunk 1 and Chunk 2).

These segments reflect NVIDIA's strategy to leverage its GPU architecture across various computationally intensive fields, including gaming, AI, and data science (Chunk 3).

Professional artists, architects and designers use NVIDIA partner products accelerated with our GPUs and software platform for a range of creative, engineering, and design use cases, such as creating visual effects in movies or designing buildings and products. In addition, generative and agentic AI is expanding the market for our workstation-class GPUs, as more enterprise customers develop and deploy AI applications with their data on-premises.

Our Businesses
We report our business results in two segments.
The Compute & Networking segment includes our Data Center accelerated computing and networking platforms and AI solutions and software, and Automotive platforms and autonomous and electric vehicle solutions including software.
The Graphics segment includes GeForce GPUs for gaming and PCs, and Quadro/NVIDIA RTX GPUs for enterprise workstation graphics.
Our Markets
We specialize in markets where our computing and AI infrastructure platforms can provide tremendous acceleration for applications. These platforms incorporate processors, interconnects, software, algorithms, systems, and services to deliver unique value. Our platforms address four large markets where our expertise is critical: Data Center, Gaming, Professional Visualization, and Automotive.
Data Center
The NVIDIA Data Center platform is focused on accelerating compute-intensive workloads, such as AI, data processing, graphics, robotics, and scientific computing, delivering superior total cost of ownership relative to conventional CPU-only approaches. It is deployed in cloud, hyperscale, on-premises and edge data centers. The platform consists of data center compute and networking infrastructure offerings typically delivered to customers as rack-scale systems, subsystems, or modules, along with software and services.
Our Data Center infrastructure systems include supercomputing platforms and servers, bringing together our higher performance, energy efficient GPUs, CPUs, interconnects, and fully optimized AI and HPC software stacks. In addition, they include a growing body of acceleration libraries, AI models and training data sets, APIs, SDKs, and domain-specific application frameworks.

Professional Visualization
We serve the Professional Visualization market by working closely with independent software vendors, or ISVs, to optimize their offerings for NVIDIA GPUs. Our GPU computing platform enhances productivity and introduces new capabilities for critical workflows in many fields, such as design, engineering, and digital content creation across a wide range of industry verticals. Additionally, the increasing number of generative and agentic AI applications is giving rise to the need for the enhanced AI and data processing capabilities of our RTX PRO GPUs.
Many leading 3D design and content creation applications developed by our ecosystem partners support RTX, allowing professionals to accelerate and transform their workflows with NVIDIA RTX PRO GPUs and software. As these applications increasingly integrate AI, these GPUs are used and leverage the same Tensor Core technology found in our Data Center solutions.

Automotive is comprised of platform solutions for automated driving from the cloud to the car. records.question: What AI-related risks does NVIDIA identify in its 10-K?
records.answer:
NVIDIA identifies several AI-related risks in its 10-K filing:

1. **Regulatory Scrutiny**: The company faces increased interest from regulators worldwide regarding its business practices in AI, which could lead to compliance costs and restrictions. This is supported by the excerpt: "Our position in markets relating to AI has led to increased interest in our business from regulators worldwide... We expect to receive additional requests for information in the future. Such requests have been and are likely to be expensive and burdensome and could negatively impact our business" (Chunk 2).

2. **Impact of Legislation**: The EU AI Act, which became effective on August 1, 2024, may affect NVIDIA's ability to train, deploy, or release AI models in the EU. This is highlighted in the statement: "Governments and regulators are also considering, and in certain cases, have imposed restrictions on the hardware, software, and systems used to develop frontier foundation models and generative AI" (Chunk 2).

3. **Infrastructure Limitations**: The availability of data centers, energy, and capital to support the buildout of NVIDIA AI infrastructure is crucial. Shortages in these resources could impact future revenue and financial performance, as noted: "The availability of data centers, energy, and capital to support the buildout of NVIDIA AI infrastructure by our customers and partners is crucial, and any shortage of these and other necessary resources could impact our future revenue and financial performance" (Chunk 3).

4. **Competition and Market Dynamics**: NVIDIA faces competition in the AI space, which could adversely impact its market share and financial results. The risk is articulated in the context of competitive pressures: "Competition could adversely impact our market share and financial results... If we are unable to successfully compete in this environment, demand for our products, services and technologies could decrease, which may negatively impact our business" (Chunk 4).

These excerpts collectively outline the various AI-related risks NVIDIA anticipates, including regulatory challenges, infrastructure constraints, and competitive pressures.

This form of AI, in which software writes itself by learning from large amounts of data, can serve as the brain of computers, robots, and self-driving cars that can perceive, understand and reason about the world. GPU-powered AI solutions are being developed by thousands of enterprises to deliver services and products that would have been immensely difficult or even impossible with traditional coding. Examples include generative AI, which can create new content such as text, code, images, audio, video, molecule structures, and recommendation systems; and agentic AI where systems of AI models work in concert to automatically complete a task.
NVIDIA has a platform strategy, bringing together hardware, systems, software, algorithms, libraries, AI models and training data sets, and services to create unique value for the markets we serve. We utilize this platform approach in each of our target markets.
Extending our technology and platform leadership in AI.
We provide a complete, end-to-end accelerated computing platform for AI, addressing both training and inferencing. This includes full-stack data center-scale compute and networking solutions across processing units, interconnects, systems, and software. Our compute solutions include all three major processing units in AI servers – GPUs, CPUs, and DPUs. These tools enable organizations to securely develop and run AI applications on NVIDIA-accelerated infrastructure anywhere.

records.question: What supply chain and manufacturing risks does NVIDIA face?
records.answer:
NVIDIA faces several supply chain and manufacturing risks, as outlined in the provided context:

1. **Availability of Resources**: The availability of data centers, energy, and capital is crucial for the buildout of NVIDIA AI infrastructure by customers and partners. Any shortage of these resources could negatively impact future revenue and financial performance (Chunk 1, Chunk 3).

2. **Complexity of Expanding Energy Capacity**: Expanding energy capacity to meet demand is described as a complex, multi-year process that involves significant regulatory, technical, and construction challenges (Chunk 1, Chunk 3).

3. **Access to Capital**: Less-capitalized companies may face difficulties securing financing for large-scale infrastructure projects, which could delay deployments or reduce the scale of AI adoption (Chunk 1, Chunk 3).

4. **Supply Constraints**: NVIDIA expects supply constraints to be a headwind to its Gaming segment in the first quarter of fiscal year 2027 and beyond, which could impact product availability (Chunk 1).

5. **Inventory Management**: The integration of new suppliers and contract manufacturers adds complexity to managing multiple suppliers, which may lead to increased inventory levels and potential inventory provisions or impairments if demand declines (Chunk 1).

6. **Manufacturing Capabilities**: NVIDIA is increasing U.S.-based manufacturing and investing in specialized equipment, but may experience delays or difficulties in scaling production as planned (Chunk 1).

7. **Long Manufacturing Lead Times**: Long lead times and uncertain supply and capacity availability can adversely affect NVIDIA's ability to meet demand (Chunk 4).

8. **Geopolitical Tensions**: Geopolitical tensions in regions where NVIDIA relies on suppliers and contract manufacturers could materially impact supply continuity (Chunk 1).

These factors collectively highlight the vulnerabilities in NVIDIA's supply chain and manufacturing processes that could affect its operational efficiency and financial outcomes.

records.question: What export control and regulatory restrictions affect NVIDIA?
records.answer:
NVIDIA faces several export control and regulatory restrictions that could materially impact its business and financial results. The key points include:

1. **Export Controls on GPUs**: The U.S. government (USG) has already imposed export controls restricting certain gaming GPUs, and there is a risk that these controls could expand to additional gaming products. This could disrupt a significant portion of NVIDIA's supply and distribution chain and negatively impact sales to markets outside China, including the U.S. and Europe (Chunk 1).

2. **Impact on AI and Data Center Products**: Export controls targeting GPUs and semiconductors associated with AI may restrict downstream users' ability to use, resell, repair, or transfer NVIDIA's products. This could negatively impact NVIDIA's business and financial results, as well as the ability of its customers to provide services (Chunk 2).

3. **Compliance Burdens**: Changes in export control rules could impose compliance burdens on NVIDIA and its customers, negatively impacting business operations. The possibility of additional export controls has already affected demand for NVIDIA's products and may benefit competitors offering alternatives less likely to be restricted (Chunk 2).

4. **Licensing Requirements**: The USG may impose licensing requirements that complicate the sale and support of NVIDIA products, potentially benefiting competitors and discouraging customers in regions like China and the Middle East from using NVIDIA products (Chunk 4).

5. **Regulatory Scrutiny**: NVIDIA is under increased scrutiny from regulators worldwide regarding its sales and competition in the GPU market. This includes inquiries from regulators in the EU, U.S., and China, which could lead to compliance costs and operational burdens (Chunk 3).

6. **Potential Financial Penalties**: There is a risk of financial penalties or restrictions on business operations if NVIDIA is found to have violated export control laws or failed to meet commitments made during acquisitions, such as the Mellanox acquisition (Chunk 2).

These factors collectively indicate that export controls and regulatory restrictions pose significant risks to NVIDIA's operational capabilities and market position.

records.question: How does NVIDIA describe its gaming segment performance?
records.answer:
NVIDIA describes its gaming segment performance by highlighting several key factors that contribute to its growth. The gaming market is characterized as the largest entertainment industry, with PC gaming being the predominant platform. Factors driving growth include new high production value games, the rise of eSports, social connectivity, and the popularity of game streamers and creators. NVIDIA's products for the gaming market, such as GeForce RTX GPUs and the GeForce NOW cloud gaming service, enhance the gaming experience with advanced graphics technology, including ray tracing and deep learning super sampling (DLSS). The introduction of the Blackwell architecture for gaming and the GeForce RTX 50 Series is also noted as a significant development, emphasizing improvements in game performance, image quality, and interactivity.

Advancing the NVIDIA accelerated computing platform.

We work to deliver continued performance leaps that outpace Moore’s Law by leveraging innovation across the architecture, chip design, system, interconnect, algorithm, and software layers. This full-stack innovation approach allows us to deliver order-of-magnitude performance advantages relative to legacy approaches in our target markets, which include Data Center, Gaming, Professional Visualization, and Automotive. Our Markets
We specialize in markets where our computing and AI infrastructure platforms can provide tremendous acceleration for applications. These platforms incorporate processors, interconnects, software, algorithms, systems, and services to deliver unique value. Our platforms address four large markets where our expertise is critical: Data Center, Gaming, Professional Visualization, and Automotive.
Data Center
The NVIDIA Data Center platform is focused on accelerating compute-intensive workloads, such as AI, data processing, graphics, robotics, and scientific computing, delivering superior total cost of ownership relative to conventional CPU-only approaches. It is deployed in cloud, hyperscale, on-premises and edge data centers. The platform consists of data center compute and networking infrastructure offerings typically delivered to customers as rack-scale systems, subsystems, or modules, along with software and services.
Our Data Center infrastructure systems include supercomputing platforms and servers, bringing together our higher performance, energy efficient GPUs, CPUs, interconnects, and fully optimized AI and HPC software stacks. In addition, they include a growing body of acceleration libraries, AI models and training data sets, APIs, SDKs, and domain-specific application frameworks.
Our networking offerings include NVLink interconnects and switches, end

AI software and NVIDIA vGPU software for graphics-rich virtual desktops and workstations.
In fiscal year 2025, we launched the NVIDIA Blackwell architecture, a full set of data center scale infrastructure that includes GPUs, CPUs, DPUs, interconnects, switch chips and systems, and networking adapters. Blackwell excels at processing cutting edge generative AI and accelerated computing workloads with market leading performance and efficiency. Offered in a number of configurations, for customers across industries and a diverse set of AI and accelerated computing use cases. In fiscal year 2026, we unveiled the NVIDIA Rubin platform, which is expected to commence production shipments in the second half of fiscal year 2027. Built for agentic AI and reasoning, it excels at processing multi-step problem-solving and massive long-context workflows, delivering up to a 10x reduction in cost per token compared to Blackwell.
For physical AI, we provide an end-to-end platform spanning data center infrastructure, open models, systems, embedded compute modules, and software stacks to train, simulate, and deploy advanced automation and robotics solutions.
Gaming
Gaming is the largest entertainment industry, with PC gaming as the predominant platform. Many factors propel its growth, including new high production value games, the continued rise of eSports, social connectivity and the increasing popularity of game streamers, modders, or gamers who remaster games, and creators.
Our products for the gaming market include GeForce RTX GPUs for gaming desktop and laptop PCs, GeForce NOW cloud gaming service, as well as SoCs and development services for game consoles.
Our gaming platforms leverage our GPUs and sophisticated software to enhance the gaming experience with smoother, higher quality graphics. NVIDIA RTX features ray tracing technology for real-time, cinematic-quality rendering, and deep learning super sampling, or NVIDIA DLSS, our AI technology that boosts frame rates while generating high-quality images for games. RTX GPUs also feature NVIDIA tensor core technology making them well suited to accelerate a new generation of on-device AI applications.
In fiscal year 2025, we announced the NVIDIA Blackwell GeForce RTX 50 Series family of desktop and laptop GPUs. The Blackwell architecture introduced neural graphics which combines AI models with traditional rendering to boost game performance, image quality, and interactivity, as well as the next generation of our DLSS technology powered by a new transformer model architecture. In fiscal year 2026, we launched and scaled Blackwell architecture for gaming and GeForce NOW.

records.question: What are NVIDIA's cybersecurity risk management policies?
records.answer:
NVIDIA has implemented several cybersecurity risk management policies designed to proactively prevent, reduce the impact of, and reactively address cybersecurity incidents. These policies include:

1. **Infrastructure and Systems**: They have established infrastructure, systems, policies, and procedures to manage material risks from cybersecurity threats. This includes following frameworks like the ISO 27001 international standard for information security management and regularly evaluating and evolving their security measures as needed (Chunk 1).

2. **Risk Assessment Processes**: NVIDIA conducts processes for assessing, identifying, and managing cybersecurity risks. They have a vendor risk assessment process that involves distributing and reviewing supplier questionnaires to evaluate cybersecurity risks associated with third parties that have access to sensitive company information (Chunk 1).

3. **Training and Policies**: The company has implemented cybersecurity and data privacy training and policies aimed at responding to new global privacy and cybersecurity laws, as well as preventing, detecting, responding to, mitigating, and recovering from significant cybersecurity threats (Chunk 1).

4. **Governance and Oversight**: Information security matters are overseen by the Board of Directors, with the Audit Committee reviewing the adequacy and effectiveness of the company's information security policies and practices. Regular updates on information security are provided to the Audit Committee and annual reports are given to the Board (Chunk 1).

5. **Consultation with Experts**: NVIDIA consults with external cybersecurity firms and risk management experts to enhance their risk management strategies (Chunk 1).

These policies reflect a comprehensive approach to managing cybersecurity risks, integrating them into the overall risk management systems and processes of the company.

Risk management and strategy
We have in place certain infrastructure, systems, policies, and procedures that are designed to proactively prevent or reduce the impact of, and reactively address circumstances that arise when, events such as a cybersecurity incident occur. Our information security management programs generally follow certain processes outlined in frameworks such as the ISO 27001 international standard for information security management and we evaluate and evolve our security measures as appropriate.

We also have a vendor risk assessment process consisting of, depending on the nature and sensitivity of the supplier and data they process on our behalf, the distribution and review of supplier questionnaires designed to help us evaluate cybersecurity risks that we may encounter when working with third parties that have access to confidential and other sensitive company information. We take steps to review that such vendors have implemented data privacy and security controls that help mitigate the cybersecurity risks associated with these vendors, depending on the nature and sensitivity of the supplier and data they process on our behalf. We routinely assess our high-risk suppliers’ conformance to industry standards (e.g., ISO 27001, ISO 28001, and C-TPAT), and we evaluate them for additional information, product, and physical security requirements.

NVIDIA pioneered accelerated computing to help solve the most challenging computational problems. NVIDIA is now a data center scale AI infrastructure company reshaping all industries.
Our technology stack includes the foundational NVIDIA CUDA development platform that runs on all NVIDIA GPUs, as well as hundreds of domain-specific software libraries, frameworks, algorithms, software development kits, or SDKs, and application programming interfaces, or APIs. This deep and broad software stack accelerates the performance and facilitates the deployment of NVIDIA accelerated computing for computationally intensive workloads such as artificial intelligence, or AI, model training and inference, data analytics, scientific computing, robotics, and 3D graphics, with vertical-specific optimizations to address industries ranging from healthcare and telecom to automotive and manufacturing.
Introduced with the Blackwell architecture, our data-center-scale offerings feature extreme co-design where the infrastructure’s chips, networking, systems, software, and algorithms are holistically architected and optimized to maximize performance and scale. Hundreds of thousands of GPUs can be interconnected to function as a single giant computer. This type of data center architecture and scale is needed for the development and deployment of modern AI and accelerated computing applications.
The GPU was initially used to simulate human imagination, enabling the virtual worlds of video games and films. Today, it also simulates human intelligence, enabling a deeper understanding of language, science, and the physical world. Its parallel processing capabilities, supported by tens of thousands of computing cores, are essential for deep learning algorithms. This form of AI, in which software writes itself by learning from large amounts of data, can serve as the brain of computers, robots, and self-driving cars that can perceive, understand and reason about the world. GPU-powered AI solutions are being developed by thousands of enterprises to deliver services and products that would have been immensely difficult or even impossible with traditional coding. Examples include generative AI, which can create new content such as text, code, images, audio, video, molecule structures, and recommendation systems; and agentic AI where systems of AI models work in concert to automatically complete a task.
NVIDIA has a platform strategy, bringing together hardware, systems, software, algorithms, libraries, AI models and training data sets, and services to create unique value for the markets we serve. We rely primarily on a combination of patents, trademarks, trade secrets, employee and third-party nondisclosure agreements, and licensing arrangements to protect our IP in the United States and internationally. Our patents and pending patent applications primarily relate to our products and the technology used in connection with our products. We also rely on international treaties, organizations, and foreign laws to protect our IP. The laws of certain foreign countries in which our products are or may be manufactured or sold, including various countries in Asia, may not protect our products or IP rights to the same extent as the laws of the United States. This decreased protection makes the possibility of piracy of our technology and products more likely. We allocate the total transaction price to each distinct performance obligation in an arrangement with multiple performance obligations on a relative standalone selling price basis. In most cases, we can establish standalone selling price based on directly observable prices of products or services sold separately in comparable circumstances to similar customers. records.question: What are NVIDIA's main product lines including H100 and Blackwell?
records.answer:
NVIDIA's main product lines include:

1. **Blackwell Architecture**: Launched in fiscal year 2025, it is a full set of data center scale infrastructure that includes GPUs, CPUs, DPUs, interconnects, switch chips, systems, and networking adapters. It excels at processing generative AI and accelerated computing workloads with market-leading performance and efficiency. In fiscal year 2026, NVIDIA also unveiled the Blackwell Ultra platform, optimized for agentic AI and reasoning (Chunk 1).

2. **H100 Tensor Core GPU**: This product is part of NVIDIA's data center offerings and is designed for high-performance computing and AI workloads. It is mentioned in the context of NVIDIA's advancements in AI and accelerated computing (although not explicitly detailed in the provided chunks, it is commonly associated with the Blackwell architecture).

3. **GeForce RTX GPUs**: These are targeted at the gaming market, including the Blackwell GeForce RTX 50 Series family of desktop and laptop GPUs, which introduced neural graphics to enhance game performance and image quality (Chunk 1).

4. **NVIDIA AI Enterprise Software**: This is a comprehensive suite of enterprise-grade AI software that supports various applications across industries (Chunk 4).

5. **NVIDIA DRIVE Platform**: This platform provides solutions for automated driving, integrating hardware and software for autonomous vehicles (Chunk 5).

These product lines illustrate NVIDIA's focus on AI, gaming, professional visualization, and automotive solutions, leveraging their advanced GPU technology.

records.question: How does NVIDIA describe the competitive significance of its CUDA platform?
records.answer: NVIDIA describes the competitive significance of its CUDA platform by highlighting its role in opening the parallel processing capabilities of GPUs to a broad range of compute-intensive applications, which paved the way for the emergence of modern AI. Specifically, it states, "With our introduction of CUDA in 2006, we opened the parallel processing capabilities of our GPU to a broad range of compute-intensive applications, paving the way for the emergence of modern AI" (Chunk 2). This indicates that CUDA is a foundational technology that enhances NVIDIA's competitive edge in AI and accelerated computing by enabling diverse applications and fostering a large ecosystem of developers. Additionally, the unified underlying programmable architecture allows NVIDIA to support several multi-billion-dollar end markets with the same technology, further reinforcing its competitive position (Chunk 2).

records.question: What are NVIDIA's customer concentration risks?
records.answer:
NVIDIA's customer concentration risks are highlighted by the significant reliance on a limited number of direct and indirect customers for revenue. For fiscal year 2026, sales to one direct customer represented 22% of total revenue and sales to another direct customer represented 14%, all primarily from the Compute & Networking segment. This trend of concentration has been consistent over the previous fiscal years, with similar high percentages for key customers. 

Additionally, the company generates a significant amount of revenue from a limited number of indirect customers, some of whom individually represent 10% or more of total revenue. This concentration could pose risks if any of these major customers were to reduce their orders or if their financial stability were to decline, potentially impacting NVIDIA's revenue and financial performance.

This includes NVLink interconnects and switches, which are part of end-to-end platforms for InfiniBand and Ethernet. The strategy aims to interconnect up to hundreds of thousands of compute nodes, facilitating the architecture of data centers that can handle AI and HPC workloads effectively.

records.question: What geographic risks does NVIDIA face related to China and Taiwan?
records.answer:
NVIDIA faces several geographic risks related to China and Taiwan, primarily stemming from export controls and regulatory scrutiny. 

1. **Export Controls**: The U.S. government has imposed export controls that restrict the sale of certain gaming GPUs and may expand these controls to additional products. This could disrupt NVIDIA's supply and distribution chain, particularly for products warehoused in and distributed from Hong Kong, negatively impacting sales not only in China but also in other markets such as the U.S. and Europe. This is supported by the following excerpt: "The USG already imposed export controls restricting certain gaming GPUs, and if the USG expands such controls... it may disrupt a significant portion of our supply and distribution chain" (Chunk 1).

2. **Impact on Demand**: Export controls may lead to a decrease in demand for NVIDIA's products, as customers outside China may seek alternatives to avoid compliance burdens. This is highlighted in the statement: "Export controls have already encouraged and may in the future encourage overseas governments to request that our customers purchase from our competitors rather than NVIDIA or other U.S. firms" (Chunk 1).

3. **Regulatory Scrutiny**: NVIDIA is under increased scrutiny from regulators in various countries, including China, regarding its sales and compliance with export controls. This scrutiny could lead to compliance costs and operational restrictions. For instance, "Governments and regulators are also considering, and in certain cases, have imposed restrictions on the hardware, software, and systems used to develop frontier foundation models and generative AI" (Chunk 3).

4. **Potential Penalties**: There is a risk of financial penalties and restrictions on business operations if NVIDIA is found to have violated laws or regulations in China. The excerpt states: "If regulators conclude that we have failed to fulfill the terms of our Mellanox acquisition... we could be subject to financial penalties, restrictions on our ability to conduct our business" (Chunk 5).

Overall, these factors indicate that NVIDIA's operations and financial results could be significantly impacted by geopolitical tensions and regulatory changes in China and Taiwan.

records.question: What are NVIDIA's main revenue streams and business segments?
records.answer:
NVIDIA's main revenue streams and business segments are divided into two operating segments: "Compute & Networking" and "Graphics." 

1. **Compute & Networking Segment**: This segment includes Data Center accelerated computing and networking platforms, AI solutions and software, and automotive platforms for autonomous and electric vehicle solutions. Overall, NVIDIA's revenue is concentrated among a limited number of direct and indirect customers, with significant contributions from both segments.

Our contracts may contain more than one performance obligation. Judgment is required in determining whether each performance obligation within a customer contract is distinct. Except for License and Development Arrangements, NVIDIA products and services function on a standalone basis and do not require a significant amount of integration or interdependency. In most cases, we can establish standalone selling price based on directly observable prices of products or services sold separately in comparable circumstances to similar customers. records.question: What AI-related risks does NVIDIA identify in its 10-K?
records.answer:
NVIDIA identifies several AI-related risks in its 10-K filing:

1. **Regulatory Scrutiny**: Increased interest from regulators worldwide regarding NVIDIA's business in AI, leading to requests for information that can be expensive and burdensome, potentially impacting business relationships.

2. **Demand for AI Services**: The demand for accelerated computing, AI-related cloud services, and large language models can fluctuate, affecting revenue.

3. **Infrastructure Limitations**: The availability of data centers, energy, and capital is crucial for building NVIDIA AI infrastructure. Shortages in these resources could delay deployments and reduce AI adoption.

4. **Export Controls**: Export controls targeting GPUs and semiconductors associated with AI could restrict the use, resale, repair, or transfer of NVIDIA products, negatively impacting business and financial results.

5. **Supply Chain Disruptions**: Potential disruptions in supply chain and distribution channels due to export controls could hinder NVIDIA's ability to meet demand.

6. **Compliance Burdens**: Repeated changes in export control rules may impose compliance burdens on NVIDIA and its customers, materially impacting business operations.

Innovation is at our core. We have invested over $76.7 billion in research and development since our inception, yielding inventions that are essential to modern computing. Our invention of the GPU in 1999 sparked the growth of the PC gaming market and redefined computer graphics. With our introduction of CUDA in 2006, we opened the parallel processing capabilities of our GPU to a broad range of compute-intensive applications, paving the way for the emergence of modern AI. In 2012, the AlexNet neural network, trained on NVIDIA GPUs, won the ImageNet computer image recognition competition, marking the “Big Bang” moment of AI. We introduced our first Tensor Core GPU in 2017, built from the ground-up for the new era of AI, and our first autonomous driving system-on-chips, or SoC, in 2018. Our acquisition of Mellanox in 2020 expanded our offerings to include networking, enabled our platforms to be data center scale, and led to the introduction of a new processor class – the data processing unit, or DPU. Over the past 5 years, we have built full software stacks that run on top of our GPUs and CUDA to bring AI to the world’s largest industries, including NVIDIA DRIVE stack for autonomous driving, Clara for healthcare, Omniverse for physical AI applications, and NVIDIA AI Enterprise software – essentially an operating system for enterprise AI applications. In 2023, we introduced our first data center CPU, Grace, built for giant-scale AI and high-performance computing, or HPC. Data Center

The GPU was initially used to simulate human imagination, enabling the virtual worlds of video games and films. Today, it also simulates human intelligence, enabling a deeper understanding of language, science, and the physical world. Its parallel processing capabilities, supported by tens of thousands of computing cores, are essential for deep learning algorithms. This form of AI, in which software writes itself by learning from large amounts of data, can serve as the brain of computers, robots, and self-driving cars that can perceive, understand and reason about the world. GPU-powered AI solutions are being developed by thousands of enterprises to deliver services and products that would have been immensely difficult or even impossible with traditional coding. Examples include generative AI, which can create new content such as text, code, images, audio, video, molecule structures, and recommendation systems; and agentic AI where systems of AI models work in concert to automatically complete a task.
NVIDIA has a platform strategy, bringing together hardware, systems, software, algorithms, libraries, AI models and training data sets, and services to create unique value for the markets we serve. While the computing requirements of these end markets are diverse, we address them with a unified underlying programmable architecture allowing us to support several multi-billion-dollar end markets with the same underlying technology by using a variety of software stacks developed either internally or by third-party developers and partners. The large and growing number of developers and installed base across our platforms strengthens our ecosystem and increases the value of our platform for our customers.

Business Strategies
NVIDIA’s key strategies that shape our overall business approach include:
Advancing the NVIDIA accelerated computing platform.
Our accelerated computing platform can solve complex problems in significantly less time and with lower power consumption than alternative computational approaches. It can help solve problems that were previously deemed unsolvable. We work to deliver continued performance leaps that outpace Moore’s Law by leveraging innovation across the architecture, chip design, system, interconnect, algorithm, and software layers. This full-stack innovation approach allows us to deliver order-of-magnitude performance advantages relative to legacy approaches in our target markets, which include Data Center, Gaming, Professional Visualization, and Automotive. While the computing requirements of these end markets are diverse, we address them with a unified underlying architecture leveraging our GPUs, CPUs, CUDA and networking technologies as the fundamental building blocks. The programmable nature of our architecture allows us to make leveraged investments in research and development: we can support several multi-billion-dollar end markets with shared underlying technology by using a variety of software stacks developed either internally or by third-party developers and partners. We utilize this platform approach in each of our target markets.
Extending our technology and platform leadership in AI.
We provide a complete, end-to-end accelerated computing platform for AI, addressing both training and inferencing. This includes full-stack data center-scale compute and networking solutions across processing units, interconnects, systems, and software. Our compute solutions include all three major processing units in AI servers – GPUs, CPUs, and DPUs. GPUs are uniquely suited to AI, and we will continue to add AI-specific features to our GPU architecture to further extend our leadership position.

records.question: What supply chain and manufacturing risks does NVIDIA face?
records.answer:
NVIDIA faces several supply chain and manufacturing risks, including:

1. **Demand Estimation Challenges**: There are difficulties in accurately estimating demand, which could become more volatile due to global and regional factors. This can lead to extended lead times and supply constraints.

2. **Supply Constraints**: Events such as natural disasters, pandemics, or geopolitical tensions can disrupt supply continuity, adversely impacting NVIDIA's operations.

3. **Increased Complexity**: The integration of new suppliers and contract manufacturers into the supply chain adds complexity in managing production planning, execution, and logistics.

4. **Inventory Management**: The expanding product portfolio and varying component compatibility may lead to increased inventory levels, which could result in inventory provisions or impairments if demand declines.

5. **Production Delays**: The complexity of product transitions and sophisticated system configurations may cause delays in production and challenges in managing supply and demand, potentially leading to revenue volatility and increased costs.

6. **Export Controls**: Restrictions on selling certain products, particularly data center GPUs, could negatively impact demand and disrupt the supply chain, especially for products warehoused and distributed from regions like Hong Kong.

7. **Regulatory Compliance Costs**: Increased scrutiny from regulators regarding competition and cybersecurity could lead to higher compliance costs and impact relationships with customers and suppliers.

8. **Security Breaches**: Breaches of security measures could expose NVIDIA and its partners to risks, including litigation, regulatory inquiries, and disruptions in operations, which could adversely affect financial results and reputation.

records.question: What is NVIDIA's research and development expenditure?
records.answer: NVIDIA has invested over $76.7 billion in research and development since its inception.
contexts: Innovation is at our core. We have invested over $76.7 billion in research and development since our inception, yielding inventions that are essential to modern computing. Our invention of the GPU in 1999 sparked the growth of the PC gaming market and redefined computer graphics. With our introduction of CUDA in 2006, we opened the parallel processing capabilities of our GPU to a broad range of compute-intensive applications, paving the way for the emergence of modern AI. In 2012, the AlexNet neural network, trained on NVIDIA GPUs, won the ImageNet computer image recognition competition, marking the “Big Bang” moment of AI. We introduced our first Tensor Core GPU in 2017, built from the ground-up for the new era of AI, and our first autonomous driving system-on-chips, or SoC, in 2018. Our acquisition of Mellanox in 2020 expanded our offerings to include networking, enabled our platforms to be data center scale, and led to the introduction of a new processor class – the data processing unit, or DPU. Over the past 5 years, we have built full software stacks that run on top of our GPUs and CUDA to bring AI to the world’s largest industries, including NVIDIA DRIVE stack for autonomous driving, Clara for healthcare, Omniverse for physical AI applications, and NVIDIA AI Enterprise software – essentially an operating system for enterprise AI applications. In 2023, we introduced our first data center CPU, Grace, built for giant-scale AI and high-performance computing, or HPC. In 2024, we launched the NVIDIA Blackwell architecture – connecting 36 Grace CPUs and 72 Blackwell GPUs in a data center scale, liquid-cooled design – for real-time trillion-parameter inference and training. In fiscal year 2026, we launched and scaled the NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra platform, optimized for agentic, reasoning, and physical AI. Business Strategies
NVIDIA’s key strategies that shape our overall business approach include:
Advancing the NVIDIA accelerated computing platform.
Our accelerated computing platform can solve complex problems in significantly less time and with lower power consumption than alternative computational approaches. It can help solve problems that were previously deemed unsolvable. We work to deliver continued performance leaps that outpace Moore’s Law by leveraging innovation across the architecture, chip design, system, interconnect, algorithm, and software layers. This full-stack innovation approach allows us to deliver order-of-magnitude performance advantages relative to legacy approaches in our target markets, which include Data Center, Gaming, Professional Visualization, and Automotive. While the computing requirements of these end markets are diverse, we address them with a unified underlying architecture leveraging our GPUs, CPUs, CUDA and networking technologies as the fundamental building blocks. The programmable nature of our architecture allows us to make leveraged investments in research and development: we can support several multi-billion-dollar end markets with shared underlying technology by using a variety of software stacks developed either internally or by third-party developers and partners. We utilize this platform approach in each of our target markets.
Extending our technology and platform leadership in AI.
We provide a complete, end-to-end accelerated computing platform for AI, addressing both training and inferencing. This includes full-stack data center-scale compute and networking solutions across processing units, interconnects, systems, and software. Our compute solutions include all three major processing units in AI servers – GPUs, CPUs, and DPUs. GPUs are uniquely suited to AI, and we will continue to add AI-specific features to our GPU architecture to further extend our leadership position.

records.question: What export control and regulatory restrictions affect NVIDIA?
records.answer:
NVIDIA has been subject to a series of shifting and expanding export control restrictions over the past three years, particularly impacting its ability to serve customers outside the United States. Key restrictions include:

1. **August 2022 Restrictions**: The U.S. government announced export restrictions targeting China's semiconductor and supercomputing industries, affecting exports of certain chips, software, hardware, and technology, specifically impacting NVIDIA's A100 and H100 integrated circuits and related systems.

2. **July 2023 Licensing Requirement**: An additional licensing requirement was imposed for a subset of A100 and H100 products destined for certain customers and regions, including some Middle Eastern countries.

3. **October 2023 Updated Licensing Requirements**: New licensing requirements were announced for exports to China and specific Country Groups (D:1, D:4, and D:5), including countries like Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Vietnam. These requirements apply to products exceeding certain performance thresholds, including various models like A100, A800, H100, and others.

4. **Impact on Business**: These export controls may disrupt NVIDIA's supply chain and distribution channels, negatively impacting its ability to meet demand, particularly in markets outside China. They may also encourage customers to "design-out" U.S. semiconductors to avoid compliance burdens, harming NVIDIA's market position and financial results.

5. **Potential Future Controls**: There is a risk of additional export controls that could further restrict NVIDIA's products, including gaming GPUs, which could significantly disrupt its operations and supply chain.

Overall, these export controls and regulatory restrictions pose significant risks to NVIDIA's business, operating results, and financial condition.

Our Markets
We specialize in markets where our computing and AI infrastructure platforms can provide tremendous acceleration for applications. These platforms incorporate processors, interconnects, software, algorithms, systems, and services to deliver unique value. Our platforms address four large markets where our expertise is critical: Data Center, Gaming, Professional Visualization, and Automotive.
Data Center

In fiscal year 2025, we launched the NVIDIA Blackwell architecture, a full set of data center scale infrastructure that includes GPUs, CPUs, DPUs, interconnects, switch chips and systems, and networking adapters. Blackwell excels at processing cutting edge generative AI and accelerated computing workloads with market leading performance and efficiency. Offered in a number of configurations, for customers across industries and a diverse set of AI and accelerated computing use cases. In fiscal year 2026, we unveiled the NVIDIA Rubin platform, which is expected to commence production shipments in the second half of fiscal year 2027. Built for agentic AI and reasoning, it excels at processing multi-step problem-solving and massive long-context workflows, delivering up to a 10x reduction in cost per token compared to Blackwell.
For physical AI, we provide an end-to-end platform spanning data center infrastructure, open models, systems, embedded compute modules, and software stacks to train, simulate, and deploy advanced automation and robotics solutions.
Gaming
Gaming is the largest entertainment industry, with PC gaming as the predominant platform. Many factors propel its growth, including new high production value games, the continued rise of eSports, social connectivity and the increasing popularity of game streamers, modders, or gamers who remaster games, and creators.
Our products for the gaming market include GeForce RTX GPUs for gaming desktop and laptop PCs, GeForce NOW cloud gaming service, as well as SoCs and development services for game consoles.

Our Company and Our Businesses
NVIDIA pioneered accelerated computing to help solve the most challenging computational problems. Since our original focus on PC graphics, we have expanded to several other large and important computationally intensive fields. Fueled by the sustained demand for exceptional 3D graphics and the scale of the gaming market, NVIDIA has leveraged its GPU architecture to create platforms for scientific computing, AI, data science, autonomous vehicles, robotics, and digital twin applications. NVIDIA is now a data center scale AI infrastructure company reshaping all industries.

Revenue growth in fiscal year 2026 was driven by data center compute and networking platforms for accelerated computing and AI solutions. Our Blackwell architectures represented the majority of our Data Center revenue.

Business Strategies
NVIDIA’s key strategies that shape our overall business approach include:
Advancing the NVIDIA accelerated computing platform.
Our accelerated computing platform can solve complex problems in significantly less time and with lower power consumption than alternative computational approaches. It can help solve problems that were previously deemed unsolvable. We work to deliver continued performance leaps that outpace Moore’s Law by leveraging innovation across the architecture, chip design, system, interconnect, algorithm, and software layers. This full-stack innovation approach allows us to deliver order-of-magnitude performance advantages relative to legacy approaches in our target markets, which include Data Center, Gaming, Professional Visualization, and Automotive. While the computing requirements of these end markets are diverse, we address them with a unified underlying architecture leveraging our GPUs, CPUs, CUDA and networking technologies as the fundamental building blocks. The programmable nature of our architecture allows us to make leveraged investments in research and development: we can support several multi-billion-dollar end markets with shared underlying technology by using a variety of software stacks developed either internally or by third-party developers and partners. We utilize this platform approach in each of our target markets.
Extending our technology and platform leadership in AI.
We provide a complete, end-to-end accelerated computing platform for AI, addressing both training and inferencing. This includes full-stack data center-scale compute and networking solutions across processing units, interconnects, systems, and software. Our compute solutions include all three major processing units in AI servers – GPUs, CPUs, and DPUs. GPUs are uniquely suited to AI, and we will continue to add AI-specific features to our GPU architecture to further extend our leadership position.
